title: Sunni and Shia
objective: After this level you can explain how a dispute over who should lead after Muhammad's death in 632 produced Islam's two main branches.
summary: After 632 most Muslims followed Abu Bakr and the caliphs (Sunnis), while others held that Ali and his descendants should lead (Shia); both share the Quran and the fundamentals of Islam.

cards.headline: One question divided Islam's two main branches: who leads now?
cards.body: When Muhammad died in 632, his followers shared the Quran and the fundamentals of the faith. What they disagreed about was who should lead the community next.

cards.headline: Two answers
cards.body: The larger group chose Abu Bakr, a close Companion of the Prophet, as caliph, and Sunnis recognize the first four caliphs as Muhammad's rightful successors. A smaller group held that leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants. The names keep the story. Shia comes from "Shiat Ali", the partisans of Ali. Sunni means one who follows the Sunnah, what the Prophet said and did.

cards.headline: Karbala
cards.body: Ali did become the fourth caliph, but he was killed in 661. In 680 his son Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with most of his companions at Karbala. Shia Muslims mourn him every year at Ashura. Most Shia, called Twelvers, recognize twelve Imams in Ali's line, the last believed hidden until he returns as the Mahdi.

cards.headline: Two branches, one faith
cards.body: Sunnis and Shia agree on the fundamentals of Islam, share the Quran, and both hold that Muhammad was the final prophet. In 2009 Pew estimated that 87 to 90 percent of the world's Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 13 percent Shia. Shia Muslims are a majority in four countries: Iran, Azerbaijan, Bahrain and Iraq. Level 4's lesson holds here too: one faith, many voices.

cards.headline: Sunni and Shia: the takeaways
learned: The branches divided over who should lead after Muhammad died in 632
Sunnis followed the caliphs; Shia held that Ali and his descendants should lead
Both share the Quran; about 87 to 90 percent of Muslims are Sunni

questions.prompt: Match each person with who they were.

pairs.right: A close Companion of the Prophet

questions.explanation: Abu Bakr was a close Companion of the Prophet, Ali was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and Husayn was the Prophet's grandson.

questions.prompt: How did the division between Sunnis and Shia begin?

options.label: In a disagreement over the text of the Quran
In a dispute over who should lead after Muhammad
In a quarrel over how many times to pray
In a debate about the date of Ramadan
options.rationale: The split was about leadership, not the calendar.

questions.explanation: The branches formed around who should lead the community after Muhammad's death in 632: Abu Bakr and the caliphs, or Ali and his descendants.

questions.prompt: Ninian Smart called every tradition a family of subtraditions. What about Islam's two branches fits that?

options.label: Shia Muslims follow a different holy book
Sunnis don't consider Muhammad to be the final prophet of God
options.rationale: Both hold that Muhammad was the final prophet.

options.label: Only Shia Muslims keep the fundamentals of Islam
They share the Quran but differ over rightful leadership

questions.explanation: Like Smart's family of subtraditions, Sunnis and Shia share the Quran and the fundamentals while differing over leadership.
